summaries.example: Imagine a class testing a paper airplane design. One flight goes badly. Instead of throwing away every idea about the plane, the class might check the folds, the paper, or the way it was thrown. If new changes lead to better and surprising flights, the design project is making progress. Lakatos thought scientific ideas often develop in a similar way.
summaries.summary: Imre Lakatos was a philosopher of mathematics and science. He argued that mathematics is not simply a finished collection of perfect rules. People often begin with an unclear idea, make a proof, find a counterexample, and then improve both the proof and the idea. He also developed the idea of a research programme in science. A programme keeps some central ideas while changing supporting ideas when tests reveal problems. It is making progress when its new versions lead to surprising predictions that observations support. Lakatos revised Karl Popper’s view that a scientific idea should be rejected as soon as it is falsified. Lakatos thought scientists can sometimes reasonably continue working on a programme with problems, especially when it is still producing useful new results. His own political life changed greatly, from early support for Stalinist communism to later opposition to Marxism and political control of scholarship. The entry also explains disagreements about how his biography, his earlier Hegelian and Marxist influences, and his later philosophy fit together.
key_ideas: Lakatos studied how mathematics and science really grow, rather than looking only at finished answers.
In mathematics, guesses, proofs, and counterexamples can improve one another.
A research programme has a central group of ideas and other ideas that can be changed to deal with problems.
A scientific programme is stronger when it makes new predictions that are later supported by observations.
Lakatos’s life included major changes in political beliefs, and people disagree about how much his early life should matter when judging his later ideas.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lakatos gives us a careful way to think about learning and discovery. A failed test does not always show that every part of an idea is useless. We can ask which part needs changing and whether the larger project is still making progress. His ideas also remind us that science is judged over time, through connected efforts, not always by one experiment or one theory alone.

important_terms.definition: A set of connected theories that share some main ideas and change over time as people try to solve problems.
A mistake, result, or example that seems to disagree with an idea.
The view that mathematics is mainly about following fixed rules from starting statements to conclusions.
Being willing to admit that our ideas can be mistaken and may need improvement.

questions_to_think_about: When should we repair an idea instead of giving it up?
Can a mistake help someone discover a better mathematical idea?
Why might a new prediction be more impressive than explaining something people already knew?
Should a thinker’s life affect how we judge the thinker’s work?

summaries.example: Consider Newtonian celestial mechanics and the unexplained shift in Mercury’s orbit. A strict, simple falsification rule might say that Newton’s theory should immediately be abandoned because its predictions did not fit the observation. Lakatos’s framework instead treats Newtonian mechanics as the hard core of a research programme, surrounded by auxiliary assumptions about celestial bodies and their motions. Scientists could investigate whether one of those assumptions needed revision. The programme would count as progressive only if such revisions produced new, successful predictions; merely inventing explanations after each failure would make it degenerating.
summaries.summary: Imre Lakatos developed a historicized account of mathematical and scientific rationality. In mathematics, he rejected the idea that finished formal derivations capture the whole intellectual enterprise. His dialogue Proofs and Refutations presents conjectures as evolving through informal proofs and counterexamples. A counterexample may force a hidden lemma into view, narrow a definition, or stimulate a stronger conjecture. Thus concepts and proofs develop together, and even an imperfect proof can contribute to rational growth. In philosophy of science, Lakatos revised Popper’s criterion that individual theories should be discarded when falsified. Scientific practice often preserves a theory’s central commitments while revising auxiliary assumptions. Lakatos therefore made the research programme the unit of appraisal. Its hard core is protected by a negative heuristic; its protective belt is adjusted under pressure; and its positive heuristic guides further development. A programme is progressive when it produces new predictions and some are confirmed. It is degenerating when it merely accommodates known problems or produces unsuccessful novelty. Scientific status is consequently a matter of degree and historical development rather than a simple logical yes-or-no property. Lakatos’s account was intended as a methodological middle way between Popper and Kuhn, though the entry emphasizes open problems, including the relation between appraisal and advice and the challenge posed by Feyerabend’s criticism that a method unable to direct scientific action may approach epistemological anarchy. The entry also treats competing interpretations of Lakatos’s political past, Hegelian influences, and the relevance of biography to intellectual history.
key_ideas: Lakatos opposed formalist, logicist, and intuitionist pictures that treat mathematics chiefly as deduction from fixed foundations. In Proofs and Refutations, he presents mathematical knowledge as developing through conjectures, informal proofs, counterexamples, and revised concepts.
A counterexample can attack a conclusion, a supporting step, or both. Rather than simply destroying a conjecture, it may reveal a hidden assumption and lead to a more precise statement.

Lakatos replaced the isolated theory as the main unit of scientific appraisal with the research programme. A programme includes a protected hard core, a revisable protective belt, and heuristics for development.

A programme is theoretically progressive when it yields new empirical content, and empirically progressive when some of that content is corroborated. A programme that repeatedly lacks such progress is degenerating.
This approach modifies Popper’s falsificationism and also offers a middle position between Popper’s emphasis on refutation and Kuhn’s emphasis on extended periods of paradigm-based work.

Lakatos used rational reconstruction to connect philosophy of science with its history, but the entry notes unresolved questions about whether this method can preserve both historical accuracy and critical evaluation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lakatos helps explain why rational inquiry is neither blind obedience to rules nor unrestricted improvisation. Scientists and mathematicians often work within traditions that contain anomalies, revise supporting assumptions, and judge success across a sequence of attempts. His framework makes prediction, historical performance, conceptual revision, and competition between programmes philosophically relevant. It also exposes a tension: a methodology may describe rational progress accurately without automatically deciding when researchers must stop, change direction, or fund an alternative.

important_terms.definition: A sequence of related theories that share central commitments and develop through changes to supporting assumptions.
The central commitments of a research programme, which its practitioners protect from direct refutation as a methodological policy.
Supporting assumptions that connect a programme’s central ideas with specific observations and predictions.
A programme’s guidance about how to develop or revise its supporting assumptions.
A programme’s policy of preserving its hard core while directing criticism toward its supporting assumptions.
The standard that a programme must generate new empirical content and receive some observational support for those new predictions.
A condition in which successive theories fail to produce successful novelty or mainly explain difficulties after they appear.
A history of ideas reconstructed as a sequence of responses that appear rational given the problems and constraints faced by thinkers.

questions_to_think_about: Is protecting a theory’s central assumptions rational persistence, or can it become a way of avoiding criticism?
Does a successful prediction support a whole research programme, or only some of its assumptions?
Should a degenerating programme be abandoned if no progressive rival is available?
Can a philosophical method both explain what scientists have done and tell us whether it was rational?
How much should biographical and political history influence interpretation of a philosopher’s published arguments?

summaries.example: Suppose a robotics club has a navigation plan for a small robot. The plan keeps a central idea about how the robot should map its surroundings, but it also uses assumptions about wheel grip, battery power, and sensor accuracy. When the robot turns incorrectly, the team does not immediately discard the central mapping idea. It changes a supporting assumption and tests the new version. The project is genuinely progressing if the revised plan predicts a new route or successful behavior that the robot then demonstrates. If the team only invents excuses after each failure, the project is degenerating.
summaries.summary: Imre Lakatos was a philosopher of mathematics and science whose work asks how rational knowledge develops over time. In mathematics, he challenged views that treat the subject as a finished system of exact deductions. His account in Proofs and Refutations shows people beginning with conjectures and incomplete proofs, then using counterexamples to uncover hidden assumptions, revise definitions, and improve arguments. A refutation may therefore help build a better idea instead of ending the entire inquiry. Lakatos’s philosophy of science develops a similar picture. Rather than judging one isolated theory, he evaluates a research programme: a sequence of related theories with a shared hard core and a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses. The negative heuristic tells researchers not to aim criticism directly at the hard core, while the positive heuristic suggests ways to develop the programme. This allows scientists to respond to anomalies without abandoning central ideas too quickly. However, not every repair is good science. A programme is progressive when later versions make new predictions and some of those predictions are supported by observation. It is degenerating when it produces no genuine novelty or repeatedly invents explanations only after difficulties appear. Lakatos therefore softened Popper’s simple falsification rule and offered a methodological alternative to Kuhn’s more sociological account of scientific change. He also argued that the history of science can test theories of rationality: a good account should make sense of important scientific achievements. key_ideas: Lakatos argued that mathematical ideas often grow through a conversation between proofs and counterexamples.
He criticized formalism because it presents mathematics mainly as deduction from already precise foundations, leaving out the process by which concepts and proofs become precise.
He revised Karl Popper’s view that a single failed prediction should quickly lead to rejection of a theory.
For Lakatos, a research programme contains a hard core and a changeable protective belt of supporting assumptions.
A programme is progressive when it predicts new facts and some of those predictions are supported. It is degenerating when it only explains familiar facts or repeatedly fails.
Lakatos’s method tries to combine logical appraisal with the history of science, while remaining different from both Popper’s and Kuhn’s approaches.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lakatos shows why intellectual progress often requires patience without permitting endless excuses. A theory may survive a problem when its wider research programme continues to generate successful, surprising results. At the same time, a programme that merely protects itself from every criticism loses its claim to rational progress. This distinction is useful for thinking about science, mathematics, education, and any long-term project where ideas must be tested and revised.

important_terms.definition: A connected series of theories that keeps some main commitments while changing other parts as problems arise.
The central ideas of a research programme, which its supporters protect while revising less central assumptions.
Extra assumptions that help a theory make specific predictions and can be changed when predictions fail.
A guide for developing new versions of a research programme.
A programme’s ability to make new predictions and receive support for at least some of them.
A programme that stops producing successful new predictions and mainly explains failures after they happen.
A historical account that shows how ideas could have been reasonable responses to the problems thinkers faced.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between intelligently revising an idea and making excuses for it?
Why might scientists continue using a theory that has encountered a problem?
Is a programme still scientific if it is currently degenerating but might improve later?
Can the history of science help us decide which ideas are rational?
Should a philosopher’s earlier political actions affect how we interpret later philosophical work?
